name: Jackson-Pratt (JP) Drain
description: Silicone drain with perforated tubing connected to a compressible bulb reservoir that creates negative pressure via suction.
normalOutput: Decreasing sanguineous to serosanguineous output over days. Typically <30 mL/day before removal.
outputColors: Serous (pale yellow/clear) - late stage, near removal
emptyingTechnique: Compress bulb completely in your hand
Open the drainage port
Allow reservoir to empty fully — measure and document output
Re-compress bulb fully before closing port to re-establish suction
Cleanse drainage port with alcohol before closing
Secure drain to patient to prevent tension/dislodgement
siteCareTips: Cleanse insertion site with NS or per order q shift
Apply dry sterile dressing if ordered
Milk/strip tubing per order to maintain patency
Secure tubing to prevent pulling
Document site appearance (no erythema, induration, leakage around site ideally)
troubleshooting: Bulb not staying compressed: check for air leak, re-evaluate seal at port
Decreased output suddenly: check for kinking, clotting in tubing — milk gently per order
Site redness/warmth/drainage around site: possible site infection — notify provider
Drain falls out or is pulled: apply pressure to site, notify provider immediately
notifyProvider: Output >100 mL/hr or sudden sharp increase in output
Output stops abruptly with distended or tender abdomen

name: Hemovac Drain
description: Flat, circular, spring-loaded reservoir (looks like a hockey puck) that creates negative pressure. Used post-orthopedic and other surgeries.
normalOutput: Sanguineous to serosanguineous, decreasing over 24–48 hours. Usually removed when output <30 mL per 8-hour shift.
emptyingTechnique: Open spout on side of reservoir
Pour contents into graduated container and measure
Completely compress the reservoir flat against a hard surface
While keeping flat, close spout — re-establishes suction
Secure drain, document output
siteCareTips: Same as JP drain — cleanse site, assess
Note suction cup appearance — should remain flat/compressed when working
troubleshooting: Reservoir expanding quickly (filling rapidly): heavy bleeding — monitor, apply pressure, notify provider
Not maintaining suction: check spout seal
Tubing clogged: gentle milking per order
notifyProvider: Bright red drainage or rapid fill
Loss of suction that cannot be restored

name: Penrose Drain
description: Flat, soft rubber drain that allows passive drainage by gravity and capillary action. Does NOT use suction. Creates a channel for fluid to escape from wound/cavity.
normalOutput: Variable — depends on indication. Can be copious initially if draining an abscess.
emptyingTechnique: No emptying — collects on dressings
Change dressings as they become saturated
Document character and estimated output from dressing weight or visualization
siteCareTips: Absorptive dressing changes per order
Safety pin through drain to prevent migration into wound
Pin should be visible and secured outside the wound
Do not advance or retract drain without order
troubleshooting: Drain migrating into wound: notify provider — safety pin prevents inward migration
Site maceration from drainage: protective barrier cream to surrounding skin
notifyProvider: Drainage suddenly stops with reaccumulation symptoms
Copious purulent drainage suggesting spreading infection

name: Chest Tube (Pleural)
description: Chest tube inserted into pleural space draining air (pneumothorax), blood (hemothorax), pleural fluid, or pus (empyema). Connected to a 3-chamber water-seal drainage system (Pleur-evac or similar).
normalOutput: Depends on indication. Expected: tidaling (fluid movement with breathing) in water-seal chamber. Fluctuating 5–10 cm with breathing is normal. Excessive bloody output (>200 mL/hr) is emergent.
emptyingTechnique: Empty drainage collection chamber per order — mark level with date/time q shift
Note total output and color
Do NOT lift the system above patient chest level — creates backflow
Keep system below chest level at all times
Document: tidaling, bubbling, output, breath sounds, SpO2
siteCareTips: Occlusive dressing at insertion site (petroleum gauze per protocol)
Never clamp chest tube except momentarily for transport or water-seal change (provider order)
Keep two clamps at bedside
Assess for subcutaneous emphysema (crepitus around insertion site)
Confirm all connections are secure and tubing not kinked
troubleshooting: Continuous bubbling in water-seal chamber (not just with exhalation): air leak — check all connections, dressing
No tidaling: lung may be re-expanded, or tube is clamped, kinked, or in wrong position — auscultate, notify provider
Clotted tube: physician/NP will assess — DO NOT milk vigorously without order
Tension pneumothorax signs (respiratory distress, tracheal deviation, absent breath sounds, hypotension): CALL CODE if tube not draining
notifyProvider: Sudden cessation of drainage with respiratory distress
Tube falls out (apply occlusive dressing, DO NOT reinsert, notify STAT)
Signs of infection at insertion site

name: Nasogastric Tube (NGT)
description: Flexible tube inserted nasally into the stomach. Used for decompression (suctioning gastric contents) or enteral feeding. May be hooked to continuous suction (Levin tube) or used intermittently.
normalOutput: For suction: 500–1500 mL/day gastric output is typical. Color: green (bile), cloudy/white (gastric secretions), coffee ground/bloody (blood — concerning).
outputColors: Bright red: active GI bleed — notify provider STAT
emptyingTechnique: Continuous low wall suction (per order): empty collection chamber q shift, document output
Intermittent suction: check per facility equipment guidance
siteCareTips: Mark tube at nostril with permanent marker — document and check each shift
Verify placement before ANY use: preferred — pH of aspirate < 5; confirmatory — chest X-ray
Check nares for pressure sores q shift — reposition tape/fixation
Keep naris moist with water-soluble lubricant
Oral hygiene q4h — patients cannot swallow normally
HOB at 30° minimum when in use
troubleshooting: Unable to aspirate: check position, try repositioning patient, flush with air
Tube coiled in mouth/throat: verify placement — may have dislodged
Bile not draining: check suction connections, kinking
Patient pulling at tube: consider mittens if ordered, educate patient
notifyProvider: Signs of aspiration (coughing, gagging, decreased SpO2 after feeding)

name: Foley Catheter (Urinary)
description: Indwelling urethral catheter for continuous urinary drainage. Inflated balloon holds catheter in bladder.
commonUses: Critically ill patients requiring hourly urine monitoring
normalOutput: Goal: ≥0.5 mL/kg/hr. Average adult: 30–50 mL/hr. Less than 30 mL/hr x 2h = oliguria — notify provider.
outputColors: Cloudy/foul odor: possible UTI — UA ordered
Orange: possible medication effect (rifampin, phenazopyridine) or bilirubin
emptyingTechnique: Empty drainage bag when 2/3 full or q shift at minimum
Measure and document output
Do not allow bag to touch floor
Always keep bag below bladder level — backflow causes infection/complications
Use clean technique with gloves when emptying
siteCareTips: Foley care q8h: cleanse urethral meatus and catheter with soap and water from meatus outward
Secure catheter to thigh — prevent tension and trauma
Assess for leaking around catheter — may indicate blockage
Maintain closed drainage system — do not disconnect
Assess for UTI signs: fever, suprapubic pain, cloudy/foul urine
Remove as soon as no longer clinically necessary — CAUTI bundle compliance
troubleshooting: No urine output: check tubing for kinking, bag position, assess bladder by palpation/ultrasound
Leaking around catheter: possible balloon deflation, bladder spasms, or wrong size — notify provider
Cloudy or bloody urine: send UA per order
Catheter falls out: apply pressure to urethral meatus if resistance felt, notify provider
notifyProvider: No urinary drainage despite patency check
